topics.title: Why does semantic HTML matter, and which elements do you actually use?
topics.html:
• Landmarks: header, nav, main (only one per page), aside, footer, section with a heading, article for standalone content. Screen reader users navigate by these, the way sighted users scan a page.
  • Headings are an outline, not font sizes: one h1, no skipped levels. Size is CSS.
  • Native interactive elements give behaviour for free: button (Enter/Space, focus, role), a for navigation, label tied to an input, details/summary for an accordion, dialog for a modal, table with th scope for real tabular data.
  • Rule of thumb: a div with an onClick needs tabindex, a role, and key handlers to match what <button> already does. Most ARIA in a codebase exists to repair markup that should have been semantic.
  • Also useful: time datetime, figure/figcaption, output, progress, template, and data-* attributes for hooks that are not styling or state.
💬 Say it like this

Semantic HTML is the cheapest accessibility and SEO work I can do. The elements carry meaning: landmarks let screen reader users jump around the page, headings form an outline, and native controls come with keyboard support and the correct role already built in.

My practical rule is to reach for the native element first. A real button gives me focus, Enter and Space, and the right role. If I use a div, I have to add tabindex, a role and key handlers just to get back to zero — and I will forget one of them.

section vs div?
A section is a part of the document with its own heading. If there is no heading and no meaning, it is a div — using section everywhere just adds noise to the accessibility tree.

topics.title: What does HTML5 give you for forms?
topics.html:
• Input types — email, tel, url, number, date, search, file, color. On mobile they change the keyboard, which is a real usability win.
  • Built-in validation — required, min/max, minlength, pattern, step. Plus the Constraint Validation API in JS: checkValidity(), setCustomValidity(), and the :invalid / :user-invalid selectors. :user-invalid is the good one — it only marks fields the user has actually touched.
  • Labels and autofill — every input needs a real label with for, and an autocomplete value so password managers and browser autofill work.
  • Other pieces: fieldset + legend for radio groups, datalist for suggestions, novalidate when you want to render your own messages, and FormData to read the whole form at submit — which is exactly how React 19 form actions work.
  • Validation on the client is UX, not security. The server validates again, always.
<form>
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required autocomplete="email" />
  <button>Sign up</button>
</form>

input:user-invalid { border-color: var(--danger); }   /* only after the user interacted */
💬 Say it like this

HTML5 already covers a lot of what people write in JavaScript. The input types give the right mobile keyboard, and attributes like required, pattern and min give validation with no code. If I need my own error messages, I use the Constraint Validation API instead of writing validation from scratch, and I style with :user-invalid so a field is not red before the user has typed anything.

Two things I always mention: every input needs a real label and an autocomplete value, and client-side validation is only user experience — the server must validate the same rules again.

topics.title: Which HTML attributes affect page loading and performance?
topics.html:
• Scripts: a plain <script> blocks HTML parsing. defer downloads in parallel and runs after parsing, in order — the safe default. async runs as soon as it arrives, in any order — for independent things like analytics. type="module" is deferred by default.
  • Images: loading="lazy" for below-the-fold images, decoding="async", explicit width and height (or aspect-ratio) to avoid layout shift, and srcset/sizes or <picture> to send a smaller file to small screens. Do not lazy-load the hero image — it is usually your LCP element; give it fetchpriority="high" instead.
  • Resource hints: preload for a critical font or hero image, preconnect for a domain you will call soon, prefetch for the next page.
  • Others: <iframe sandbox> and rel="noopener noreferrer" on external links, meta viewport for mobile, and <link rel="preload" as="font" crossorigin> plus font-display: swap to avoid invisible text.
💬 Say it like this

The main one is script loading: a normal script tag blocks parsing, so I use defer by default, which keeps execution order but does not block the HTML parser, and async only for independent scripts like analytics.

For images I set width and height so nothing jumps, lazy-load everything below the fold, and use srcset so phones do not download a desktop-size file. The one exception is the hero image — it is usually the largest contentful paint element, so it must not be lazy; I give it high fetch priority and sometimes preload it.

Why noopener on target="_blank"?
Without it the opened page gets a reference to your window through window.opener and can redirect it to a phishing page. Modern browsers do this by default, but the attribute is still the safe habit.
